title: The wars
hook: France's religious wars raged around his tower, and he talked peace to both sides

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the daughters: one passing sentence that readers still wonder about. Your line was hidden grief.

A country house in France. Outside, armed bands from two sides of a civil war over religion ride the roads. Neighbors bar their gates, hire guards, and sleep badly. One house leaves its gate open. Inside, in a tower, a man is writing a book about himself. He belongs to one of the two churches and doesn't hide it. And men on both sides use him to carry word between them. Today, how Montaigne lived in the middle of a war about faith.
screen: `A CIVIL WAR OVER RELIGION.` → `ONE GATE LEFT OPEN.` → `WORD CARRIED BETWEEN THEM.`

segments.voice: First, the open gate. While others fortified their homes, Montaigne writes, he kept his unguarded, with only a porter at the door, more for old custom and ceremony than for defense. A guarded house, he reasons, invites attack, because it looks like a prize. His stayed open, and he says it was spared. Second, how he talked. In the essay Of the useful and the honest, he describes going between great men on opposite sides. He tells each plainly what he'd tell the other, and doesn't pretend to belong to the side he doesn't. Because he wasn't playing a game, people trusted him with their real thoughts. Third, his candle. He'd gladly carry a candle to Saint Michael, he says, and another to his dragon. It's a joke with an edge, told against himself: he'll follow his own side even to the fire, but not into it if he can help it. Fourth, the cost. In a later essay he admits moderation got him beaten from every side: one camp took him for the enemy, and the other camp did the same. Talking to both often makes both suspicious. He did it anyway, out loud, in his own name. The wars near us are smaller: two siblings, two friends who stopped speaking. His way isn't pretending they agree. It's keeping the gate open and saying the same true thing in both rooms.
screen: `AN OPEN GATE, A LONE PORTER.` · `THE SAME WORDS TO EACH SIDE.` · `A CANDLE FOR THE SAINT AND DRAGON.` · `SUSPECTED BY BOTH.` · then, large: `TALK TO BOTH.`

segments.voice: Pick a small quarrel you're near, not necessarily in. Picture the first person and silently say one true thing you'd be willing to say to them; then picture the second, and say the same thing. Notice where the words wanted to change, to flatter one side or cut the other, and keep them the same.
The wars. France's wars of religion, which Montaigne lived through with his gate open, saying the same plain words to both sides. Today's word.
Your line: talk to both. It cost him trust on both sides, and he kept at it. That's today, done.

chat.says: During France's religious wars, did Montaigne pretend to agree with both sides?
options: No; he kept his own side openly, but told each side the same plain things.
Yes; he told each side what it wanted to hear, to keep his house safe.
No; he stayed silent and refused to speak with either side at all.
chat.meaning: Montaigne didn't hide which church he belonged to, but told great men on both sides the same plain words, so both trusted him with their real thoughts.

porter.meaning: a doorkeeper at a gate or entrance

Saint Michael.meaning: the archangel shown defeating a dragon in Christian art

moderation.meaning: keeping to the middle; avoiding extremes

sources.ref: Essays 2.15, That our desire is increased by difficulty (his house left unguarded during the civil wars, with only a porter)
Essays 3.1, Of the useful and the honest (dealing openly between princes; a candle to Saint Michael and one to his dragon)
Essays 3.12, Of physiognomy (moderation made him suspect to both parties)

notes: All Montaigne passages paraphrased. Confirm each attribution: open house (2.15), candle to Saint Michael and his dragon (3.1), suspected by both sides as Guelph to the Ghibellines and Ghibelline to the Guelphs (3.12).
The 'candle' line in 3.1 is said with irony and in a particular context; confirm the gloss 'he held to his own side, but refused to treat the other as monsters beyond reason' is fair.
'A round tower' and 'south of France' are general descriptions of his estate; the tower library is described in Essays 3.3. Cut if the claims editor wants only the text.
No dates, numbers of wars or names of princes given, by design.
